title: The wrongdoer wrongs himself
hookLine: whoever does wrong, wrongs himself first (Meditations 9.4)

cards: Someone cuts you off in traffic, then makes a rude gesture for good measure. In the moment there's only one victim, and it's you. But follow that driver home.

The rest of their evening is still inside that anger. Their shoulders are still up; their day is still a little worse for it. Marcus wrote a very short entry in book nine about exactly this, two lines long.

teach.h: WRONG DONE IS WRONG TO ONESELF.
teach.b: In George Long's 1862 translation: “He who does wrong does wrong against himself.” Then Marcus adds: whoever acts unjustly acts unjustly toward himself, because he makes himself bad.
For Marcus, the only real harm is harm to your character, the ruling part of you.

teach.h: ONLY YOU CAN DAMAGE YOUR GOODNESS.
teach.b: Your car, your schedule, even your body can be damaged by someone else. Your goodness can be damaged only by you. So the person who wrongs you has, at most, dented your fender.
They've dented their own self. If that's true, the wrongdoer isn't someone to hate.
They're someone to pity, the way you'd pity a person who stepped on their own foot and then blamed the floor. That isn't looking down on them. It's seeing the injury clearly.

teach.h: NOT DOING CAN BE UNJUST, TOO.
teach.b: The very next entry keeps this honest: a person can act unjustly by not doing something, too. So pity is no reason to stand by; standing by can be a wrong of its own.

What shifts is the feeling underneath. Not, how dare they, but what did that cost them? And by Marcus's logic it cuts close to home: every time we snap, cheat, or lie, the first person changed is the one who did it.

how: Readers of Marcus often use this line to turn anger toward someone who wronged them into something closer to pity, while still acting to protect themselves and others.

games.q: the wrongdoer wrongs himself — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus says the wrongdoer is harmed first, by becoming worse
acting unjustly, he writes, makes oneself bad.
the idea means we should never step in when someone does wrong
the very next entry says we can be unjust by not acting, too.

games.q: someone cheats you out of something small. you're Marcus. how do you look at them?
o: as someone who has hurt themselves first.
as someone not worth a thought.
games.why: Marcus writes that whoever does wrong, wrongs himself, because he makes himself bad. the feeling that follows is closer to pity than hate.

practice: Bring to mind someone who wronged you, a small or middle-sized wrong, not your deepest wound.
Picture them afterward: the evening that followed, what they had to tell themselves, what kind of person that act made them a little more of.
See if a sliver of pity shows up beside the anger; it doesn't excuse them, it just sees them.

wordCard.voice: George Long, whose translation gives Marcus's short entry: he who does wrong does wrong against himself, and makes himself worse. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to do wrong, to err. Marcus's line turns on this verb.

carryVoice: Your line: he's hurt himself. Pity sees the injury without excusing it. Day six hundred eight, done.
